locator: Section 2 'Replicated state machines', p.1
claim: Raft's Section 2 defines replicated state machines as state machines on a collection of servers that compute identical copies of the same state and keep operating even when some servers are down.
quote: Consensus algorithms typically arise in the context of replicated state machines. In this approach, state machines on a collection of servers compute identical copies of the same state and can continue operating even if some of the servers are down.

locator: Section 2 'Replicated state machines', p.2 (the example paragraph)
claim: Section 2's opening example is large-scale systems with a single cluster leader (GFS, HDFS, RAMCloud) that use a separate replicated state machine to manage leader election and store configuration that must survive leader crashes, citing Chubby and ZooKeeper.
quote: For example, large-scale systems that have a single cluster leader, such as GFS [8], HDFS [38], and RAMCloud [33], typically use a separate replicated state machine to manage leader election and store configuration information that must survive leader crashes. Examples of replicated state machines include Chubby [2] and ZooKeeper [11].

locator: Section 2 'Replicated state machines', p.2
claim: The consensus module on a server accepts commands from clients into its log and communicates with the other servers' consensus modules so that every log eventually holds the same requests in the same order, even if some servers fail.
quote: The consensus module on a server receives commands from clients and adds them to its log. It communicates with the consensus modules on other servers to ensure that every log eventually contains the same requests in the same order, even if some servers fail.

locator: Abstract, p.1
claim: For understandability, Raft separates consensus into the key elements leader election, log replication, and safety, and reduces the number of states to consider.
quote: In order to enhance understandability, Raft separates the key elements of consensus, such as leader election, log replication, and safety, and it enforces a stronger degree of coherency to reduce the number of states that must be considered.

locator: Section 2.1 'The Problem', p.1
claim: Lamport's three safety requirements are: only a proposed value may be chosen, only a single value is chosen, and a process never learns a value was chosen unless it actually was.
quote: The safety requirements for consensus are: Only a value that has been proposed may be chosen, Only a single value is chosen, and A process never learns that a value has been chosen unless it actually has been.

locator: Section 2.4 'Progress', p.7
claim: When two proposers each complete phase 1 with successively increasing proposal numbers, the lower-numbered proposer's phase-2 accept requests are ignored because the acceptors promised not to accept anything numbered below the higher number, so neither proposal is chosen.
quote: Proposer p completes phase 1 for a proposal number n1. Another proposer q then completes phase 1 for a proposal number n2 > n1. Proposer p's phase 2 accept requests for a proposal numbered n1 are ignored because the acceptors have all promised not to accept any new proposal numbered less than n2.

locator: Section 2.4 'Progress', p.7
claim: The fix for the dueling-proposer livelock is to guarantee progress by selecting a distinguished proposer as the only one that tries to issue proposals.
quote: To guarantee progress, a distinguished proposer must be selected as the only one to try issuing proposals.

locator: 'Failures', first paragraph
claim: The FLP result shows that in an asynchronous model consensus cannot be solved even if just one server stops (crashes).
quote: even a single stop failure makes the consensus problem impossible to solve. This is the famous Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (“FLP”) impossibility result

locator: 'References'
claim: The FLP result was published by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson in JACM 32(2), April 1985.
quote: Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process. Michael J. Fischer, Nancy A. Lynch, and Michael S. Paterson. JACM 32(2), April 1985.

locator: Chapter 9 'Leader election evaluation', p.117 (opening paragraph)
claim: Because FLP rules out deterministic termination in a purely asynchronous model, Raft relies on randomized election timeouts rather than a termination guarantee.
quote: According to the FLP impossibility result [28], no fault-tolerant consensus protocol can deterministically terminate in a purely asynchronous model.

locator: Section 3.9 'Timing and availability', p.27
claim: Raft gives up timing-independent liveness: its safety never depends on timing, but availability (responding to clients in a timely manner) inevitably does.
quote: One of our requirements for Raft is that safety must not depend on timing: the system must not produce incorrect results just because some event happens more quickly or slowly than expected. However, availability (the ability of the system to respond to clients in a timely manner) must inevitably depend on timing.

locator: Section 5.6 'Timing and availability', p.10
claim: Raft requires broadcastTime much less than electionTimeout much less than MTBF, stated as the timing requirement in Section 5.6.
quote: Raft will be able to elect and maintain a steady leader as long as the system satisfies the following timing requirement: broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF

locator: Section 3.9 'Timing and availability', p.28
claim: broadcastTime much less than electionTimeout keeps heartbeats arriving before followers time out and also makes split votes unlikely; electionTimeout much less than MTBF keeps the system making steady progress.
quote: The broadcast time should be an order of magnitude less than the election timeout so that leaders can reliably send the heartbeat messages required to keep followers from starting elections; given the randomized approach used for election timeouts, this inequality also makes split votes unlikely. The election timeout should be a few orders of magnitude less than MTBF so that the system makes steady progress.

quote: A log entry is committed once the leader that created the entry has replicated it on a majority of the servers (e.g., entry 7 in Figure 6).

locator: Section 5.4.3 'Safety argument', p.9 (point 2, Figure 9)
claim: Because the majority that stored the entry and the majority that elected the later leader overlap, at least one server both holds the committed entry and voted for that later leader, so the entry survives later elections.
quote: leaderT replicated the entry on a majority of the cluster, and leaderU received votes from a majority of the cluster. Thus, at least one server (“the voter”) both accepted the entry from leaderT and voted for leaderU

locator: 'What is maximum cluster size?'
